![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226336/assets/172737d1a5b28b9a60958dc7e6b1748db1912021b7df4ad26045648063037fd8.png)

The area of one loop of the polar curve $r=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta +\frac{\pi }{4})$ (shown above) is given by the integral

$$
A=\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{-3\pi /8}^{\pi /8}{cos}^{2}⁡(2\theta +\frac{\pi }{4})\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Which of the following represents the total area bounded by the polar curve?
question.worked_solution:
The given polar curve is the polar rose with $2\cdot 2=4$ petals, and we know that the area of the first petal is

$$
A=\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{-3\pi /8}^{\pi /8}{cos}^{2}⁡(2\theta +\frac{\pi }{4})\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

The $1$st petal is traversed from ${\theta }_{1}=-\frac{3\pi }{8}$ to ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{8},$ and the length of this interval is $\frac{\pi }{2}.$

To find the interval for the second petal, we have to add $\frac{\pi }{2}$ to both ends of the interval of the first petal:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{3} & ={\theta }_{1}+\frac{\pi }{2}=-\frac{3\pi }{8}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{\pi }{8} \\ {\theta }_{4} & ={\theta }_{2}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{\pi }{8}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{5\pi }{8}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, to obtain the interval for the third petal, we add $\frac{\pi }{2}$ to both ends of the interval of the second petal:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{5} & ={\theta }_{3}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{\pi }{8}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{5\pi }{8} \\ {\theta }_{6} & ={\theta }_{4}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{5\pi }{8}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{9\pi }{8}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to obtain the interval for the fourth petal, we add $\frac{\pi }{2}$ to both ends of the interval of the third petal:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{7} & ={\theta }_{5}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{5\pi }{8}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{9\pi }{8} \\ {\theta }_{8} & ={\theta }_{6}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{9\pi }{8}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{13\pi }{8}\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, we obtain the following intervals for all $4$ petals of our rose:

$$
{{[-\frac{3\pi }{8},\frac{\pi }{8}]}_{⏟}}_{1\text{st}},\,{{[\frac{\pi }{8},\frac{5\pi }{8}]}_{⏟}}_{2\text{nd}},\,{{[\frac{5\pi }{8},\frac{9\pi }{8}]}_{⏟}}_{3\text{rd}},\,{{[\frac{9\pi }{8},\frac{13\pi }{8}]}_{⏟}}_{4\text{th}}
$$

Therefore, the total area of the given polar curve can be obtained if the curve is traversed from $\theta =-\frac{3\pi }{8}$ to $\theta =\frac{13\pi }{8}:$

$$
{A}_{\text{total}}=\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{-3\pi /8}^{13\pi /8}{cos}^{2}⁡(2\theta +\frac{\pi }{4})\,\text{d}\theta 
$$
